hints.title: Test the two implications separately
hints.body: For sufficiency, begin with equal endpoint heights and ask whether the required interior horizontal tangent must occur. For necessity, begin with an interior horizontal tangent and ask whether the endpoint heights must match.
hints.recap: Necessary and sufficient describe opposite implication directions.
hints.pitfall: Do not judge both directions from one sketch.
hints.pause: Write down the two implications before investigating either one.

recall.reminder: Necessary and sufficient describe opposite implication directions.

hints.title: Use heights and gradients carefully
hints.body: Sketch a smooth polynomial joining two points of equal height. Consider both a constant graph and one that departs from that height. Then test the reverse implication with a simple quadratic and an interval whose endpoints are not symmetric about its vertex.
hints.recap: A stationary point concerns gradient; equal endpoint values concern height.
hints.pitfall: The stationary point must be strictly inside the interval, not at an endpoint.
hints.pause: Explain the behaviour between equal heights and calculate a separate example to test the reverse implication.

recall.reminder: A stationary point concerns gradient; equal endpoint values concern height.

solution:
1. Test sufficiency. Suppose p(a)=p(b). If p is constant on this interval, its derivative is zero at every interior point. Otherwise, the continuous polynomial graph takes some interior value above or below the common endpoint height. It therefore attains an interior maximum or minimum, where its derivative is zero. So equal endpoint heights are sufficient.

2. Test necessity. Take p(x)=x2, a=−1 and b=2. The derivative is p′(x)=2x, so the interior point c=0 satisfies p′(c)=0. However, p(−1)=1 and p(2)=4, so the endpoint values differ.

3. Classify the condition. It is sufficient but not necessary.

Answer C.
knowledgePattern: Test both directions between equal polynomial endpoint heights and an interior stationary point
